question: What is the meaning of rigidity in relation to resistance and rigidity?
description: Rigidity in the context of materials science refers to the material's resistance to deformation under applied forces. It is a measure of a material's stiffness or its ability to maintain its shape when subjected to stress. Rigidity is an important property in construction materials as it determines how well a material can support loads and maintain structural integrity. In the context of resistance and rigidity, rigidity is the material's ability to resist bending, stretching, or compressing forces, thereby maintaining its original shape and dimensions. This property is crucial for ensuring the stability and durability of construction materials and structures.

v. GIS-based MPs 
As indicated in the theme analysis and study categorization, some researchers employed Geographic Information Systems 
(GIS) to develop MPs. To achieve this, a GIS model, which encompasses groups of BIM models at various locations, is used to 
collect data about building materials [16,62]. Schaubroeck et al. [62] presented a system for modelling building connections 
and optimising disassembly sequences using GIS-based MPs that are connected to BIM. The method encourages the reuse and 
recycling of pre-existing construction materials by assessing the flow of recovered resources and their potential for circular 
buildings. In order to evaluate the possibility of circularity based on factors including cost, time and environmental impact, the 
approach involved collecting detailed data on building assembly and placing a strong emphasis on Product Material Passports. 
The innovative part of the framework was a combination of the Disassembly Sequence Planning (DSP) model, which is essential 
for detecting components that need complicated arrangements during disassembly [62]. Following a similar approach, Entrop 
[16] investigated how to use GIS technology to improve circularity in infrastructure restoration projects. The study offered a 
theoretical framework for effective road material management that links MPs to GIS. As it was emphasised the implementation 
of laser scanning and ground penetration radar (GPR) are very advantageous for collecting data without the need of distractive 
intrusion. This could be a milestone for infrastructure projects, as making it possible to determine the types of materials, 
pavement and subsurface conditions, which are all essential for maximising road maintenance and, at the same time, reducing 
the negative environmental effects of the project [16].
